header.tag_why: The CFO compared only rate lines and called us 'the same thing'. We never turned the one-in-twelve checkout failure into a Fernbrook figure he could see, even though Farah offered the analysis and Lucy asked for a one-page business case.

messaging_changes.current_line: Customers see an average uplift in authorization rates with Authorization Boost and Adaptive Acceptance.
messaging_changes.change: For ecommerce buyers losing high-value orders at checkout: "Stop your big orders dying at the last step. We'll show you why your large baskets get declined, what those failed orders are worth, and what we change to win them back." Keep the average uplift (Authorization Boost / Adaptive Acceptance) only as supporting proof under this line, never as the headline value claim.
messaging_changes.why: The customer's pain was one in twelve orders failing, worst on big baskets, with no explanation from the processor, and she described it as 'orders dying at the last step'; our average-uplift slide was what we leaned on, and it did not carry the case.

messaging_changes.current_line: Proven ROI, backed by an independent economic impact study.
messaging_changes.change: For the CFO or finance approver, especially when they won't meet us and the champion has to carry the case: "Your ROI in your numbers: we run your own decline export and put the value of your failed orders next to your total payment cost, on one page you can hand your CFO." Make this one-pager the standard answer to 'something I can hand my CFO' instead of the deck and pricing proposal.
messaging_changes.why: Lucy asked for something to hand Martin and got the deck and the pricing proposal. We skipped Farah's offer to analyse their declines, so the CFO decided on a rate-only page and saw 'the same thing'.

messaging_changes.change: Counter line for when an incumbent bank or processor sharpens its rate: "A better rate on the same failed orders is still losing you orders. Here's what your declines cost next to the rate difference." Use it to pull the conversation back from rate to the cost of declines before the customer's finance team builds a rate-against-rate comparison.
messaging_changes.why: When the bank cut its rate, the conversation moved from declines to 'can you do better on the rate', and the deal was decided on a side-by-side rate page. We had no line to bring it back to the failed orders.

trigger.insight: This was a revenue-loss problem with a measured rate from the customer's own dashboard, concentrated on the highest-value orders. It was never a pricing evaluation. The incumbent's weakness was opacity ('no straight answer on why'), and that is exactly what a rate cut doesn't fix. We had the customer's own metric in hand from day one and never turned it into money.
trigger.messaging: Open decline-driven deals with 'what are your failed orders worth and why are they failing', not M1's global positioning. Make diagnosis the hook: 'we'll tell you why your big orders fail.'

decider.insight: The CFO decided alone, and we never met him. Everything we know about his reasoning comes through Lucy. We accepted 'she'd carry it' without arming her: she carried a deck and a quote into a room where the controller had built the frame. IT made itself conditional on finance, so finance was the only gate that mattered, and it was the one we had no direct line to.
decider.messaging: When the economic buyer won't meet us, the champion's leave-behind is our pitch. Every deal needs a CFO-ready one-pager in the buyer's numbers, not a deck.

competitor.insight: The bank's counter was a rate cut and nothing more. It worked because it moved the conversation from declines (our ground) to rate (theirs), and we followed: we answered rate emails with a pricing proposal instead of pulling back to the cost of failed orders. 'No new product, nothing' is the rep's commentary. It is actually our best argument, since a cheaper rate on the same one-in-twelve failure is still losing orders, but we never put that to the customer.
competitor.messaging: Add an incumbent-bank counter play: when the bank sharpens the rate, respond with 'a better rate on the same failed orders' and show the decline cost against the rate difference.

message.insight: The reaction came from Farah explaining why Fernbrook's big-ticket orders get declined, a customer-specific diagnosis. The generic M4 average uplift didn't land, and it is what we leaned on 'a lot'. The silence question was never really answered. The real silence was the CFO, who never heard the decline story from us at all.
message.messaging: Lead with the specific diagnosis Farah gave ('why your large orders get declined, and what we change'), and use the M4 average only as support, never as the value claim.

decided.insight: It was lost on a page the controller built: rate against rate, with our quote as the only thing from us on it. Price is the symptom. 'The same thing' means the CFO saw no difference in what he'd get, because nobody showed him the failed orders. The rep himself conceded that matching the rate would have left a page saying 'same rate, so why move', so the rate-only diagnosis doesn't hold. Lucy's 'formality' read shows the champion also misjudged the CFO.
decided.messaging: Never let a rate-only comparison be the decision document. Ship a total-cost-plus-recovered-revenue page before the customer's finance team builds their own.

gaps.insight: This wasn't a product gap. It was a proof gap we chose. The customer explicitly asked for a CFO business case, and we had a way to build one (Farah's decline analysis), but skipped it because of quarter-end timing. Our substitute was customer stories and an average uplift (M6/M8-style generic proof), which is exactly what reads as 'the same thing' to a CFO. Gateway fees and chargeback headcount never reached the page either.
gaps.messaging: Make a 'cost of your declines' one-pager (failed-order value from the customer's export, plus total payment cost beyond the statement rate) the standard response to 'something I can hand my CFO', and retire the deck as that answer.

language.insight: The champion talks in lost sales and wasted effort ('orders dying', 'the card says no' on a greenhouse). Our language is 'authorization rates' and 'uplift', which a CFO hears as an abstract percentage. Martin's 'the same thing' is reported in two different wordings, so treat it as a strong paraphrase, but either way it shows our differentiation never reached him.
language.messaging: Rewrite M4 in customer language, e.g. 'stop big orders dying at the last step', and express acceptance as recovered order value rather than an average uplift percentage.

gaps.question: What did Martin actually have in front of him about the cost of one-in-twelve failed orders?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Lucy: did the decline problem and its cost come up in the meeting with Martin, or was it only the rate page?

gaps.question: Was the gateway fee or the chargeback headcount on the controller's one-pager?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Lucy what the one-pager contained, and whether we can see it or have it described.

gaps.question: What exactly did Martin say? Two wordings were reported.
gaps.follow_up: Ask Lucy for Martin's words as closely as she remembers them, and what he meant by 'the same thing'.

gaps.question: Which parts of the pitch got silence?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Farah, who was in the sessions, which topics drew no questions or interest from Lucy or IT.

gaps.question: How far apart were our rate and the bank's sharpened rate?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Sam or deal desk for both figures, to test whether 'more room on the rate' was even plausible.

gaps.question: Did the spring timing and the IT lead's nervousness shape the CFO's no?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Lucy whether a post-spring start would have changed the conversation, and whether the failure rate is still running at one in twelve, so we can reopen with Farah's decline analysis.

close.rep_takeaway: When the champion asks for 'something I can hand the CFO', that is the deal asking you for its decision document. Build it in their numbers (Farah's decline analysis on their own export), even if it costs two weeks at quarter-end. Otherwise their controller builds it for you, and it will only have the rate on it.
